item.title: Italy ’s Parliament Under Cyber Pressure: Why the Attack on the Chamber Matters
item.description:
Italy ’s Parliament cyberattack highlights hybrid warfare risks and the need for transparency, stronger defenses and accountability.

The cyberattack targeting email accounts at Italy’s Chamber of Deputies, including a parliamentary account assigned to Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, raises questions that go well beyond the security of individual inboxes. At a time when European institutions face growing cyber pressure, the incident highlights how access to political communications can become part of a broader hybrid warfare strategy.

The Chamber confirmed that its IT systems had been targeted and said it had activated security measures in cooperation with Italy’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN). According to reports, three parliamentary email accounts were affected, including those associated with Meloni, former Justice undersecretary Andrea Delmastro and lawmaker Paolo Formentini.

Palazzo Chigi clarified that the account assigned to Meloni was not the one she uses for government communications. That distinction matters, but it does not settle the broader security questions raised by the incident. The public information available so far does not provide a complete technical account of what happened, what level of access the attackers may have obtained, or whether any information was taken.

The Chamber described the incident as having no emergency implications, adding that attacks of this kind occur daily. It also confirmed that similar attempts and pressure on IT systems had intensified in recent days, affecting other Italian, European and international institutions.

This combination of statements deserves closer scrutiny. Cyberattacks may be a daily occurrence, but their frequency does not make every incident routine or harmless. The significance of an attack depends on the target, the access obtained, the information exposed and the wider strategic context.

An email account is more than a channel for exchanging messages. It can reveal professional relationships, contacts, ongoing discussions, schedules and the way an institution operates. Depending on the level of access obtained, an attacker may also find documents, personal information or details that could help target other officials.

A compromised account can provide a starting point for further attacks. Messages sent from a legitimate address may appear trustworthy, making it easier to approach colleagues, political staff or external partners. Information gathered from correspondence can also support impersonation, targeted phishing or attempts to obtain access to other systems.

Even an account that is not used for government business can therefore have intelligence value. The important question is not simply whether an account handles classified information, but what an attacker could learn from it and how that information might be used.

The distinction between an attempted attack and a confirmed compromise is equally important. Public statements have not yet provided enough technical detail to establish the full extent of the incident. Investigators need to determine whether access was blocked, whether an account was accessed, whether messages were read and whether credentials or other information were exposed. These are different scenarios, with different implications for security.

The incident should also be considered against the backdrop of growing cyber pressure on public institutions. On October 8, Italy’s Foreign Ministry was targeted by a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack that media reports linked to pro-Russian actors. A DDoS attack and an intrusion targeting email accounts are technically different operations, and there is currently no public evidence linking the two incidents.

Their broader significance, however, lies in the pressure they place on institutions and the range of objectives that cyber operations can serve.

Hybrid warfare does not rely on a single method. It can combine cyber operations, intelligence gathering, propaganda, disinformation, economic pressure and other activities designed to exploit weaknesses or influence decision-making. These actions do not necessarily need to be coordinated in every case to contribute to a more hostile strategic environment.

In this context, a cyber operation does not need to shut down a public service to have an impact. An attacker who gains access to political correspondence may seek information about relationships between officials, internal priorities or ongoing discussions. That information could potentially support intelligence operations, help prepare future intrusions or provide material for influence campaigns.

Stolen communications can also be selectively leaked, manipulated or presented without context to damage reputations and undermine public trust. The value of such material may lie less in its immediate technical impact than in how it can be used later. These are possible scenarios, not established facts about the attack on the Chamber.

The public perception of an incident can itself become part of the problem. A successful intrusion, if confirmed, can raise doubts about an institution’s ability to protect sensitive communications. A poorly handled response can deepen those doubts, particularly if officials appear more concerned with reassuring the public than explaining what happened.

None of this proves that the attack was directed by a foreign government or formed part of a coordinated influence operation. Attribution requires technical evidence, intelligence and careful analysis. Treating hybrid warfare as a serious risk means investigating these possibilities without presenting them as conclusions before the evidence supports them.

The Chamber’s statement that the incident was not an emergency because similar attacks occur daily is, at best, an inadequate explanation of the risk. It confuses the frequency of attacks with the seriousness of their potential consequences.

Reassurance has a legitimate role in crisis communication. Institutions should prevent unnecessary alarm and explain when protective measures are working. But reassurance is not a substitute for transparency, especially when the technical investigation is still underway.

The Chamber has acknowledged that cyber pressure has increased against other institutions in Italy and abroad. That admission makes it even more important to explain the nature of the threat and the measures being taken to address it.

A responsible update should clarify what is known about the affected systems, which protective controls were activated, what investigators have established and which questions remain open. Sensitive technical details can be withheld when their disclosure could compromise an investigation or expose additional weaknesses. That does not justify treating the incident as unremarkable before its impact is understood.

The response also needs to go beyond public statements. Authorities should review access controls, authentication mechanisms, account monitoring, email forwarding rules and the procedures used to detect suspicious activity. They should assess whether accounts that are no longer needed remain active and whether older accounts receive the same protection and monitoring as those used every day.

The objective is not to assume that a dormant account caused the incident, but to ensure that every account represents only an acceptable level of risk.

The attack should prompt a broader review of how parliamentary communications are protected and how cyber incidents are handled. New agencies, appointments and organizational structures can contribute to security, but they do not guarantee it. Their value depends on clear responsibilities, technical expertise, adequate resources, tested response procedures and measurable results.

Cooperation between the Chamber and the ACN is important, but the public also needs a clear account of how the incident is being investigated and what corrective action follows. Where the investigation establishes weaknesses, those weaknesses must be addressed rather than obscured by general assurances.

The challenge is particularly significant as Italy and other European countries prepare for future elections. Political institutions may face not only attempts to disrupt their services but also operations intended to collect information, exploit internal divisions or influence public debate. Cybersecurity is therefore part of democratic resilience, alongside the ability to identify manipulated information, communicate reliably and maintain public confidence.

The first priority must be to establish what happened at the Chamber and avoid unsupported claims about the attackers’ identity or objectives. The next is to use the findings to strengthen the security of parliamentary communications and other institutional systems.

An institution’s response should be judged not by its claims that an attack is under control, but by its ability to establish what happened, communicate the risks clearly and fix the weaknesses identified. As hybrid threats grow, downplaying an incident before its implications are fully understood sends the wrong message: protecting the institution’s public image appears to take precedence over identifying and reducing the risks.

item.title: Three Japan-Focused Cyberattacks Show How Hackers Use AI
item.description:
Three Japan-focused cyberattacks show how AI helps hackers scale operations, while exploiting old systems and weak security remains key.

In autumn 2026, Japanese companies and other organizations reported a series of data leaks involving their web systems. On October 9, Japan’s National Cybersecurity Office issued a warning to businesses, while the head of the ruling party’s cybersecurity team described cyberspace as being in a “state of emergency.”

Researchers at Trend Micro studied three attack infrastructures to understand how hackers use AI. Their findings show three different approaches, ranging from limited AI assistance to systems that use AI agents to manage almost an entire attack.

The researchers looked at files that attackers left on servers anyone could reach. These included attack scripts, lists of targets, logs, and records of commands. The files showed attacks on organizations in Japan and other countries.

But the researchers could not see the victims’ own logs or network records. So they could not confirm every break-in, measure the full damage, or say who was behind it.

Attackers also like to claim more success than they really had. The researchers only counted a result as real when the evidence backed it up.

The three cases show that AI does not play the same role in every cyberattack.

“The cases differ along two dimensions: how much of the attack AI handled and how confidently we can establish its involvement.” reads the report. “Case A used AI to drive the entire workflow, which we confirmed. Case B was human-led, with confirmed AI assistance in planning and tool development. Case C showed high-confidence indications of AI use in a limited role, such as tool development. All three were active in 2026, and much of the activity preceded the previously published ARTEX reports.”

Case A: AI agents managed the attack workflow. The researchers confirmed the use of CyberStrikeAI, an open-source penetration-testing platform built around AI agents. It handled reconnaissance, vulnerability checks, exploitation, data theft and reporting as part of a repeatable process.

The platform split tasks among multiple AI agents. One record mentioned a credential-search agent in a system that used 44 agents. The platform could also generate Japanese content, including forms and fake login pages.

Researchers identified at least 19 target organizations, including at least 16 in Japan. The system worked on several targets at once and kept traffic to each organization relatively low. This made the activity harder to detect by checking the logs of a single victim.

Despite this automation, the platform rarely gained deep access to target systems. In many cases, it had no active session or web shell and showed no evidence of stolen data. The clearest intrusion started through an administration page that was publicly accessible on an old web system. The attackers did not need to exploit a newly discovered vulnerability.

Case B: A human attacker used AI to plan and build tools. In this case, the operator made the main decisions but used a large language model to speed up planning and tool development. The researchers found an attack plan written by an LLM that targeted services providing AI and GPU resources.

The attacker presented requests as authorized security testing to get around the model’s safety limits. The researchers say this was a false claim, although they did not publish the exact method.

The attacker also targeted AI infrastructure, including platforms for AI workflows, data processing and model inference. The researchers believe the goal may have been to gain access to computing resources that could be used to run AI models cheaply.

Some intrusions had serious consequences. In one case, the attacker gained control across several systems, including an FTP service, a database, an administrator account, a web shell and SSH access. The attacker also restored backdoors after they had been removed.

In another case, a geographic information system server was exposed with default credentials. This provided access to hundreds of thousands of land and business records, as well as Windows credentials and email data. The evidence confirmed that information was downloaded.

However, the researchers found no evidence that AI carried out these attacks independently. It helped the operator plan and build tools, while the actual work relied mainly on scripts, existing software and human decisions.

Case C: AI played a limited role. Here, the operator appears to have used AI mainly to develop tools and scripts. The researchers found no evidence that it was involved in planning or managing the wider operation. They rated AI involvement as highly likely, but not confirmed, because they found no direct evidence such as prompts or API keys.

The operator ran at least six campaigns in 2026, targeting exposed VPN devices and Oracle WebLogic servers. The targets included devices from Cisco, Citrix, F5 and Yamaha.

In attacks against Yamaha RTX1210 routers, the operator did not exploit a product vulnerability. Instead, the attacker used credentials found in configuration files. These credentials provided direct access to internal corporate networks.

The researchers also found signs that AI may have helped write some commands and scripts. These included unusually structured comments and emoji used as status markers. Such clues can support an assessment, but they cannot prove AI use on their own.

Japan was the main target in all three operations, but attackers also targeted other countries and regions. All three used Simplified Chinese, but this does not prove they came from the same group or location.

“Simplified Chinese was the working language in all three infrastructures. Japan was the largest target country, although the operators also pursued nearby countries and regions. Entry points were exposed legacy systems or weaknesses left in default configurations.” concludes the report. “Target selection was opportunistic across industries: the operators sought systems that were easy to attack from outside and acted on what they found.”

The main difference was how AI was used. In one case, AI agents managed much of the attack and worked on many targets at once. In another, AI helped a human plan attacks and build tools. In the third, AI was mainly used to develop tools.

AI helped make attacks faster and easier to scale, but attackers still exploited familiar weaknesses, such as outdated web systems, exposed admin pages, default passwords and poorly secured network devices. Researchers also found that AI tools sometimes reported planned actions as successful, making it essential to verify their results.

AI can also help defenders discover vulnerabilities. However, researchers found no evidence that these three operations used AI-discovered zero-day flaws. Their attacks relied on known vulnerabilities and poor security settings.

The report identifies six main priorities for defenders:

  • Review public-facing systems. Identify old web applications and update them or isolate them if they cannot be secured.
  • Protect administration pages. Check that management interfaces are not exposed to the internet without a clear need and strong access controls.
  • Secure VPNs and network devices. Review configurations, remove default credentials and check for reused passwords.
  • Protect internal AI services. Include AI workflows, inference services and GPU systems in asset inventories, and check whether they are exposed.
  • Improve monitoring. Look for low-volume attacks spread across many targets, which may be difficult to spot in the logs of a single organization.
  • Prepare for AI misuse. Organizations that use LLMs for work should train staff to recognize requests that falsely claim to be authorized security testing.

These security weaknesses existed long before AI became widely available. AI simply helps attackers find and exploit them faster and across more systems.

The time between discovering a vulnerability and using it in an attack may also become shorter. Organizations should install security updates quickly and apply temporary protections when patches are not available.

Researchers still don’t know who was behind the three operations, whether they were connected or how much damage they caused. Further reports may provide more answers.

“The attackers’ identities, whether the three cases share an operator, the full scale of the damage, and the AI models used remain unresolved. Our observations come from attacker-side files and still require confirmation from the affected organizations.” concludes the report. “We are considering further technical reporting on individual cases: AI-driven activity in Case A, AI assistance in Case B, and limited AI assistance in Case C. We will also continue working with the relevant organizations.”

The main lesson is clear: AI can make cyberattacks faster and larger, but the basic security priorities remain the same. Organizations must identify systems exposed to the internet, strengthen access controls and detect suspicious activity before attackers turn a simple weakness into a serious breach.

item.title: U.S. CISA adds Google Brotli and Adobe Commerce and Magento flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
item.description:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Google Brotli and Adobe Commerce and Magento flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Google Brotli and Adobe Commerce and Magento vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

Below are the flaws added to the catalog:

  • CVE-2026-111497 (CVSS score: 9.2) – An unchecked return value vulnerability in Google Brotli that could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to corrupt decoder memory, expose sensitive information, cause a denial-of-service, or potentially execute arbitrary code by sending a specially crafted Brotli-compressed stream.
  • CVE-2026-48356 (CVSS score: 9.3) – An unrestricted file upload vulnerability in Adobe Commerce and Magento that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the current user, potentially gaining elevated access or taking control of the victim’s account or session.

Brotli is a data-compression algorithm developed by Google.It reduces the size of web content, such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and other text-based resources. Security researchers have observed exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-111497 (aka Node2Shell), a critical flaw in Google’s Brotli library. Previdian recorded one attempt by October 27, while ELLIO researchers recently detected traffic carrying a public exploit that could execute code on vulnerable systems. The activity may indicate attempts to exploit the flaw on a larger scale, but its scope remains unclear. An attacker can trigger the vulnerability to cause crashes, expose sensitive memory or remote code execution when applications decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data. Because Brotli is widely used, multiple projects and vendors have released security updates, including Node.js, PHP, Bun, and Microsoft .NET. Cybersecurity firm Wiz warned that 91% of cloud environments contain resources vulnerable to the flaw, while 82% have publicly exposed Node.js instances.

The second flaw added to the catalog is an unrestricted file upload vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-48356, dubbed PolyShell. Recently WordPress security firm Sansec warned of attacks exploiting CVE-2026-48356 to infect at least 953 of online stores. The attackers reportedly used a Magento CMS block to insert a malicious loader capable of retrieving and executing a payload hosted under their control.

So far, researchers have not recovered the subsequent payload, leaving the campaign’s ultimate objectives unclear. The activity is believed to have been underway since at least July 2025 and remains ongoing.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the flaws by October 29, 2026.

  • CVE-2026-111497 (CVSS score: 9.2) – An unchecked return value vulnerability in Google Brotli that could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to corrupt decoder memory, expose sensitive information, cause a denial-of-service, or potentially execute arbitrary code by sending a specially crafted Brotli-compressed stream.
  • CVE-2026-48356 (CVSS score: 9.3) – An unrestricted file upload vulnerability in Adobe Commerce and Magento that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the current user, potentially gaining elevated access or taking control of the victim’s account or session.

Brotli is a data-compression algorithm developed by Google.It reduces the size of web content, such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and other text-based resources. Security researchers have observed exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-111497 (aka Node2Shell), a critical flaw in Google’s Brotli library. Previdian recorded one attempt by October 27, while ELLIO researchers recently detected traffic carrying a public exploit that could execute code on vulnerable systems. The activity may indicate attempts to exploit the flaw on a larger scale, but its scope remains unclear. An attacker can trigger the vulnerability to cause crashes, expose sensitive memory or remote code execution when applications decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data. Because Brotli is widely used, multiple projects and vendors have released security updates, including Node.js, PHP, Bun, and Microsoft .NET. Cybersecurity firm Wiz warned that 91% of cloud environments contain resources vulnerable to the flaw, while 82% have publicly exposed Node.js instances.

The second flaw added to the catalog is an unrestricted file upload vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-48356, dubbed PolyShell. Recently WordPress security firm Sansec warned of attacks exploiting CVE-2026-48356 to infect at least 953 of online stores. The attackers reportedly used a Magento CMS block to insert a malicious loader capable of retrieving and executing a payload hosted under their control.

So far, researchers have not recovered the subsequent payload, leaving the campaign’s ultimate objectives unclear. The activity is believed to have been underway since at least July 2025 and remains ongoing.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the flaws by October 29, 2026.

item.title: CVE-2026-97631: 16-Year-Old UEFI Flaw Threatens Servers (2026)
item.description:
CVE-2026-97631: A 16-year-old UEFI flaw (CVSS score of 9.5/10) enables pre-OS code execution. Exposed servers need firmware patches and checks.

A critical flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97631 (CVSS score of 9.5), in the firmware that boots most of the world’s servers is now public, and the patch details came out months early.

The bug affects TianoCore EDK II, an open-source project used by hardware manufacturers and cloud providers to build UEFI firmware. UEFI is the software that starts a computer before the operating system loads. EDK II is widely used across the industry, including by major UEFI vendors such as AMI, Insyde and Phoenix. Even Microsoft’s more secure version, Project Mu, used the vulnerable component.

“EDK2 contains a vulnerability in BIOS where a user may cause “Out-of-bounds Write”, Classic Buffer Overflow, and “Incorrect Calculation of Buffer Size” by remote access. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability can lead to arbitrary code execution. It could also impact Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability.” reads the advisory.

The flaw can corrupt memory in a component that handles ICMP messages, which devices use to report network errors. Attackers could exploit it to run code before the operating system starts and before security protections such as Secure Boot are fully active. Secure Boot checks that the software loaded during startup can be trusted, while the Trusted Platform Module (TPM) supports security functions such as hardware-based trust. Although the attacker’s code does not remain active after execution, it could help attackers install other malicious components that run early in the boot process.

The flaw is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe). That driver lets servers, storage gear and other devices boot from code downloaded over a local network. While it does that, it listens for ICMP errors, and it never enforces the 504-byte limit on how much it copies.

“While a machine is PXE-booting over IPv4 or IPv6, an unauthenticated network attacker who can deliver ICMP error messages to it can corrupt DXE-phase memory and execute arbitrary code before the operating system loads, before Secure Boot or measured boot has verified or measured any OS component.” states the advisory.

A malicious insider, or a hacker with low-level access to the local network, can send an error message that spills code past the limit and corrupts the UEFI module running on the CPU.

The advisory is more precise. The driver keeps a receive request open for ICMP errors and copies each message into a fixed 504-byte field called Mode.IcmpError. In both the IPv4 and IPv6 handlers (PxeBcIcmpErrorDpcHandle and PxeBcIcmp6ErrorDpcHandle) the bounds handling is wrong: a longer message still gets copied, and the destination pointer moves by the cumulative length and not the per-fragment length. So an oversized message writes attacker-controlled bytes past the field, and nothing earlier on the receive path limits its size.

The attack is simple. The attacker sends a direct message to the target’s IP address during the PXE boot process, even from a remote network. Sending invalid data can stop the boot process and cause a denial of service. If the attacker knows the target’s firmware version, they can create a fake event to run their own code at ring 0, the CPU’s highest privilege level. This also bypasses attestation, which uses cryptographic checks to prove that the hardware is trustworthy. As a result, the attack can help an attacker turn limited access into full control.

The attacker needs some control over the local network. This could be an insider or an external attacker who already has a foothold in the target network and is seeking to gain higher privileges. So far, there’s no evidence that this flaw can be exploited to gain initial access to a network from the outside.

The flaw affects some systems that start up over a network using EDK2-based firmware with PXE enabled. Home and small-office users, and anyone who boots only from a disk drive, aren’t affected.

Researchers planned to disclose the bug in January, but AMI published a fix last month, revealing details of the flaw. TianoCore then issued a public warning. Attackers can now study the fix to develop exploits, while updating firmware across many devices could take a long time.

It’s still unclear which devices are affected. Intel and Arm say their own products aren’t directly affected, but manufacturers may add vulnerable code. Several other companies hadn’t answered questions when the article was published.

Organizations should contact their system or firmware supplier and disable network boot where possible. They should also monitor logs for suspicious activity. TPM and Secure Boot remain useful protections, but they don’t stop this attack.

item.title: Ads or Surveillance? Researchers Flag Suspicious Targeting of Starlink Users
item.description:
Discover-Tech allegedly targeted Starlink users with digital ads to track their locations, according to sources cited in a new Reuters report.

Digital defense firm TrendAI found that an Israeli ad tech company was heavily targeting users of satellite internet service Starlink, probably to spy on them. That’s according to six people familiar with the matter, speaking to Reuters. Raphael Satter reported it on October 27 in a Reuters story, and the claims rest on sources, not on a published attribution.

“Researchers at TrendAI, a unit of Tokyo-based cybersecurity company Trend Micro, ‌concluded the Israeli company Discover-Tech was one of the biggest sources of digital ads shown to users of SpaceX’s Starlink service and that the ads were likely being used to geolocate or otherwise surveil them, according to the six people.” Reuters states.

TrendAI concluded that the company Discover-Tech was one of the biggest sources of digital ads shown to users of SpaceX’s Starlink. They believe the ads were likely used to geolocate users or otherwise surveil them.

“TrendAI™ Research observed large-scale use of advertising infrastructure for geolocation tracking, advertising technology surveillance, and intelligence gathering. Data from these activities is valuable for precise targeting of key individuals in sensitive locations, including active conflict zones.” reads the report published TrendAI. “SHADOW-EARTH-79 is also the number one bidder in 105 individual countries in Starlink traffic that we observed. It accounts for approximately 13% of all winning bid events in Starlink traffic, five times higher than average (approximately 3%) bids for other bidders, and the highest of any high-volume buyer. Starlink is widely used in conflict zones where terrestrial networks are degraded.”

SpaceX didn’t respond to requests for comment, and Discover-Tech and its chief executive didn’t respond over the past two weeks.

Starlink users make attractive targets. Governments around the world are trying to get a grip on satellite internet terminals, which route data through SpaceX satellites and not through nationally regulated telecom firms. That lets them sidestep local internet restrictions, work in hostile areas or coordinate action across battlefields. Ukraine’s military relies on Starlink for frontline communications and for directing drone strikes.

The findings come from advertising data collected by TrendAI. The data shows that Discover-Tech became one of the biggest bidders for ads shown to Starlink users worldwide. It was the top bidder in more than 100 countries, including several where Starlink is banned or restricted. Advertisers bid in online auctions to buy space for ads in browsers and apps.

“In Starlink IP space traffic that we observed, SHADOW-EARTH-79 is the second-largest winning bidder by raw volume. However, examining the statistics and saturation of the group’s ad impression buying strategy reveals an obvious skew towards buying ad impressions on Starlink addresses, compared with its overall footprint.” continues the report.

TrendAI published its report on October 15 but didn’t name Discover-Tech. Instead, it identified “an ad tech entity” called Shadow-Earth-79. Six sources say that’s TrendAI’s codename for Discover-Tech.

TrendAI didn’t directly explain why it left out the company’s name. It said its naming policy helps prevent mistakes and avoids labels that could confuse security teams, lead them to focus on the wrong risks or prompt the wrong response.

Starlink users are valuable targets for surveillance. Governments want more control over satellite internet services, which send data through SpaceX satellites rather than local telecom networks. Starlink lets users get around local internet restrictions, stay connected in dangerous areas and communicate on the battlefield.

Ukraine’s military uses Starlink for frontline communications and to help direct drone strikes.

Finding ways to track Starlink users has turned into a cottage industry. In May, the Israeli newspaper Haaretz and the website Intelligence Online separately reported that Israeli-owned businesses were pitching clients on ways to identify and track them. Haaretz said exploiting ad data appeared to play a key role.

On the same day as TrendAI’s report, the Canadian cyber watchdog Citizen Lab and the New York ad tech firm Confiant named Discover-Tech. Both said it abused the ad bidding process, which can leak data about internet users back to the bidder. Over time, a bidder can collect that data, collate it and merge it with other information to de-anonymize users and follow them around the web. In some cases it can also set them up for targeting with surveillance software.

Citizen Lab and Confiant said the ads appeared inside dozens of sensitive networks belonging to media organizations, governments and tech firms. Google, Comcast and other companies said they removed Discover-Tech from their ad platforms. At least one big US tech company and one international organization recently started internal inquiries into whether Discover-Tech’s ads targeted their employees, according to one of the six people and a seventh person familiar with the matter.

TrendAI’s report pointed to suspicious bidding patterns that suggested “targeting and tracking infrastructure” and not a commercial advertising operation.

“Overall, the design of this “customer-facing” front-end makes us believe that the system is more likely designed as a “surveillance” and “intelligence gathering” platform, rather than simply a platform for advertisement management.” the report concludes. “The collected evidence indicates with moderate-to-high confidence that SHADOW-EARTH-79’s advertising presence functions as targeting and tracking infrastructure rather than a commercial advertising operation. The anomalous bidding behavior, heavy dominance in sanctioned and conflict states, and pronounced over-bidding for Starlink address space establish intent to reach specific audiences in sensitive geographies.”

It noted an obvious skew toward Starlink-aimed ads. It also found that Shadow-Earth-79 was the top ad buyer in Syria, Libya, Yemen and South Sudan, and the second biggest in Afghanistan. Few Western brands are chasing shoppers in Libya at the moment, and the report says demand for legitimate Western advertising in sanctioned or active-conflict states is effectively zero.

The entity also won an implausibly dominant share of bids in several other countries, including Hungary, Israel, Egypt, Azerbaijan and Venezuela. The researchers were convinced Discover-Tech was behind it and discussed naming it in the report, according to the six sources. They dropped the idea after TrendAI executives raised legal concerns, five of those sources said.

It wouldn’t be the first time. Earlier this year, Reuters reported that Palo Alto stripped explicit references to China from a report on a global cyberespionage campaign, even though its researchers were confident Beijing was behind the hacking. Reuters said the report was watered down over fears that naming China would cause problems for Palo Alto’s operations there, which were already under scrutiny after a Beijing directive told domestic companies not to use its products. Palo Alto said the lack of attribution had nothing to do with China’s procurement rules and called any suggestion otherwise speculative and false.

Executives fear that exposing surveillance operations could draw retribution, and industry experts tell Reuters the sector has a habit of staying quiet.

“Self-censorship is common in the cybersecurity industry, especially when executives fear that exposing surveillance operations could draw retribution, industry experts say.” Reuters concludes.

item.title: Hive and Nefilim Ransomware Affiliate Gets 70 Months In Jail
item.description:
Artem Stryzhak gets 70 months in prison for Hive and Nefilim ransomware attacks, while the FBI offers $11 million for his alleged co-conspirator.

A federal court in Brooklyn has sentenced Artem Stryzhak, a Ukrainian national, to 70 months in prison for using ransomware to extort millions of dollars from victims. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York announced it in a press release, and it also says an $11 million reward remains for a co-conspirator who’s still at large.

“Earlier today, in federal court in Brooklyn, Artem Stryzhak, a Ukrainian national, was sentenced by United States District Judge Pamela K. Chen to 70 months in prison for using ransomware to extort millions of dollars from victims.” reads the DoJ’s press release. “The defendant pled guilty in December 2025 to conspiracy to commit fraud, extortion, and related activity in connection with computers.  “

In December, Artem Aleksandrovych Stryzhak pleaded guilty in the U.S. for Nefilim ransomware attacks. The Ukrainian citizen was arrested in Spain in 2024 and extradited to the US in April 2025. He pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit computer fraud, extortion, and related activity

Nefilim ransomware was used to encrypt networks worldwide, including in the Eastern District of New York, causing millions in losses from ransom payments and system damage. Attackers employed a customized ransomware executable in each attack, generating unique decryption keys and tailored ransom notes for victims. In June 2021, Nefilim administrators granted Artem Stryzhak access to the ransomware code in exchange for 20% of his ransom proceeds, which he deployed via his account on the administrators’ online platform.

Stryzhak and co-conspirators researched victims using online databases to collect information on their net worth, size, and contacts. After gaining network access, they stole data to pressure companies into ransom payments. Nefilim notes warned that stolen data would be posted on publicly accessible “Corporate Leaks” sites maintained by the administrators if victims did not comply.

Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, Stryzhak’s co-defendant and Nefilim admin, is a serial ransomware cybercriminal who is still at large. 

According to court documents, his first role was with Nefilim. Starting around June 2021, he joined the ongoing Nefilim conspiracy as an affiliate and got access to the ransomware. In exchange, he agreed with one of the group’s administrators, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, to pay the administrators 20 percent of the ransom proceeds. Even crime has licensing fees.

One of those attacks came in June 2021, when Stryzhak stole data from a company in the oil and gas transportation industry. About a week later, he created email addresses that went into a ransom note sent to the victim. He kept deploying Nefilim ransomware through at least October 2021.

Separately, he also joined the Hive ransomware group as one of its earliest affiliates. From June 2021 to January 2023, Hive’s conspirators attacked about 1,500 victims worldwide, including government entities, hospitals and businesses. The attacks caused major disruption to daily operations around the world and affected responses to the COVID-19 pandemic. One hospital had to give up digital technology to treat its patients and couldn’t take in new ones right after the attack.

As a Hive affiliate, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators hit seven victims, including law firms, a dentist’s office and a healthcare provider, during the pandemic. Those victims couldn’t get to their encrypted data. The FBI, as part of a months-long effort to disrupt Hive, gave a decryption key to one of Stryzhak’s victims, so that victim recovered its data without paying a ransom.

U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella, Jr. thanked the FBI’s New York Field Office, the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs and its Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, and Spanish law enforcement for helping to capture him.

“Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc—harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors,” stated United States Attorney Nocella. “Today’s sentence reflects that cybercriminals cannot hide from law enforcement and will face significant punishment for their criminal conduct. We remain determined to capture Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, a serial ransomware developer and Stryzhak’s co-conspirator.”

The State Department’s Transnational Organized Crime Rewards Program is offering up to $11 million for information that leads to the arrest, conviction or location of Tymoshchuk.

Anyone with information can call the FBI at +1-917-242-1407 or email [email protected], contact a local field office if in the United States, or reach the nearest U.S. Embassy if overseas.

item.title: Virtualine Domain Seized, but Allegedly Abusive Website Remains Online
item.description:
The FBI seized Virtualine, a hosting service accused of supporting criminal sites, ignoring abuse reports and helping launder money from illegal activities

The FBI seized the website of Virtualine, a hosting service that sold its services to criminals. The seized domain is virtualine.net, and the government says the site was used to commit and facilitate prolific criminal activity. That includes the advertisement of sexually explicit images of minors, the intentional disclosure of nonconsensual intimate images of adults and minors, and international money laundering. A court authorized the seizure.

“Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, and Darren B. Cox, Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI Washington Field Office, announced today the seizure of the website virtualine.net after it was used to commit and facilitate prolific criminal activity, including the advertisement of sexually explicit images of minors, the intentional disclosure of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions of adults and minors, and international money laundering designed to conceal and promote criminal conduct.” The Justice Department has the details in a press release.

Virtualine, also known as Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo and Omegatech, offers “bulletproof” hosting. It sells hosting, servers and domain names to customers who want a provider that ignores abuse complaints. It promotes its services on cybercrime forums.

Court records include examples of those ads. In September 2024, Virtualine told an Exploit.in user that it allowed illegal activities such as phishing, payment card fraud, email spam and port scanning, but banned child sexual abuse material and terrorism-related content. In June 2025, it boasted on HackForums that it ignored more abuse than three therapists combined.

In March 2026, Virtualine promoted an “additional protection plan” for customers, offered after the company received an official request from law enforcement. Under the plan, it would move the customer’s criminal infrastructure to another shell company unaffiliated with Virtualine, and then reactivate the server. It was a game of musical shell companies.

“In March 2026, Virtualine advertised its “additional protection plan,” which it offered to its customers after “receiv[ing] an official request from law enforcement agencies.” Under this plan, Virtualine would move the customer’s criminal infrastructure to “another shell company not affiliated with Virtualine, after which the server is reactivated.”” continues the press release.”As Virtualine advertised to users on the platform HackForums in June 2025, “Virtualine ignored more abuse than your last three therapists.””

Despite saying it bans child content, the government says Virtualine knowingly hosted a website that carried it. Court records call that site Vendor 1. It’s a criminal online forum where users post and sell access to nude, sexually suggestive or sexually explicit images and videos of minors and adults, and it also promotes a hack-for-hire service in which people pay hackers to get into victims’ online accounts without consent and take explicit images and videos.

In January 2026, about a month after assigning Vendor 1 an IP address, Virtualine began receiving reports of child sexual abuse images and videos on the server. The reports came from police in Germany, Canada and Australia, the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and a victim’s lawyer. According to the government, Virtualine continued hosting Vendor 1 despite those warnings.

The government also says Virtualine helped Vendor 1 build a new website. It allowed users to upload illegal material and download it after paying.

The site accepted several payment methods, including an option called “BTC [NO-AML].” It used bitcoin addresses outside a hosted payment service, allowing customers to pay directly and avoid that service’s checks for illegal funds.

Authorities say some payments came directly from criminal groups. They accuse Virtualine of accepting the money and moving it through further transactions to hide its source.

The FBI’s Washington Field Office led the investigation, with significant help from Germany’s Polizei Hessen, the Netherlands’ Politie Midden-Nederland, the U.K.’s National Crime Agency, and private partners OverRIPE and Lumen. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs also assisted. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Laura D. Withers and Stefanie A. Schwartz represent the government.

A domain seizure doesn’t end the problem, and the government says so in plain terms. The new website Virtualine built with Vendor 1 has already drawn at least one abuse complaint about sexually explicit images of children, and the release adds: Virtualine hosts this new website to this day.

item.title: ENGIE Data Breach Exposes Customer Details and Energy Contracts
item.description:
ENGIE says attackers accessed French customers’ contact and energy contract data through a partner sales tool. Banking data was not affected.

French multinational energy company ENGIE warned customers in France that attackers accessed personal information through a sales tool used by some business partners. The exposed data includes contact details and energy contract information that could help fraudsters impersonate the supplier.

The company says its internal IT systems weren’t compromised and banking information wasn’t affected. It has blocked the attackers’ access, notified the relevant authorities and contacted affected customers, according to a spokesperson who spoke to BleepingComputer.

According to notification emails sent to affected customers, the incident involved a tool used by partners to sell the company’s electricity and natural gas offers.

The notification confirms that attackers gained unauthorized access to personal information stored in the sales tool.

“We are informing you that an act of cyber-malice recently affected a tool used by some of our partners to market energy offers. As part of this incident, unauthorized access to your personal data was identified.” reads the notification.

The compromised information includes customers’ names, postal addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers, customer IDs, contract numbers and energy supply identifiers.

The company hasn’t disclosed the partner or platform involved. It also hasn’t revealed how many customers were affected, when the intrusion began, or when it was discovered.

For electricity customers, these include the delivery point identifier (PDL). For gas customers, they include the metering and estimation point (PCE).

ENGIE says financial information wasn’t affected and that its investigation indicates the exposure was limited to contact details and certain contract information.

That reduces one category of risk but doesn’t eliminate financial fraud. Attackers can use accurate customer information to persuade victims to disclose additional data or make payments.

Anyway, the exposed data could support impersonation scams. The company warned customers to watch for attempts to obtain further information or induce payments. A contract number, however, doesn’t prove that a caller is legitimate. It may simply show that the person has access to an exposed record.

Customers should verify unexpected requests through trusted channels, even when the sender knows their personal details.

ENGIE hasn’t attributed the attack to a specific group, and at this time no ransomware group has claimed responsibility for the attack.

Experts recommend visiting ENGIE’s official website or app directly instead of signing in through links received by email.

Customers should also be cautious with unexpected calls and messages. If someone requests a payment, password or additional personal information, they should end the exchange and verify the request using independently obtained official contact details.

Customers should never share SMS verification codes, passwords or banking details with someone who contacts them unexpectedly.

item.title: Election Website Security: 42% of US County Sites Still Lack .gov Domains
item.description:
US election websites show improved security, but weak email protection, non-.gov domains and third-party tracking still expose voters to risks.

Millions of Americans will use websites to check their registration, find polling places or track ballots before the November 3 election. However, a new study finds that many county election websites still have security weaknesses involving domain names, email authentication, encrypted connections and third-party tracking.

Mysterium VPN’s 2026 County Election Website Security Census examines 2,081 county election websites across the United States.

“42% of county election websites aren’t on .gov (869 of 2,081 identified). That’s down from 57% in 2024.” states the report. “Weighted by population, it’s 28% because the big counties moved first.”

That’s an improvement from 57% in the company’s 2024 census. However, the findings reveal persistent weaknesses that could expose voters to impersonation, misleading websites and unnecessary data collection.

These findings concern public information websites and their contact domains. They do not establish that voting machines, ballot-counting systems or election results have been compromised.

The researchers started with 3,144 US counties and county equivalents but identified county-run election information pages for 2,081. Of these, 869 used domains outside .gov.

Only verified US government organizations can register a .gov domain, making it a useful way for voters to identify official government websites. The study found that larger counties had made more progress: when weighted by population, 28% of residents lived in counties whose election pages used non-.gov domains.

Texas accounted for 169 non-.gov sites, including 134 using the older co.<county>.tx.us structure. Arizona and Nebraska had no identified non-.gov county election sites.

The FBI and CISA previously warned that criminals were using fake election websites to spread false information and collect personal data. Moving to .gov and redirecting older addresses can reduce confusion, although the domain alone cannot guarantee that every aspect of a website is secure.

Election offices communicate with voters about registration, identification requirements and missing ballots. Weak email authentication can make it easier for attackers to impersonate these offices.

Of 1,977 readable election pages, 965 displayed a contact address. After excluding consumer email services, researchers examined 942 county-controlled domains.

“Of the 1,977 election pages whose content we could read, 965 display a contact address. Twenty-three of those are at consumer providers like Gmail. As in 2024, we set them aside, because Gmail’s security policy is Gmail’s, not the county’s.” states the report. “That leaves 942 county-controlled election email domains.”

The study reported that 23% had no DMARC record, while 28% used p=none, a monitoring-only policy that does not request quarantine or rejection of unauthenticated messages. Another 30% requested quarantine and 19% rejection.

Together, the first two groups account for roughly 51% of domains without an enforced DMARC policy. The report’s underlying counts total 941 rather than the stated 942, a discrepancy that requires clarification.

The share of domains without DMARC fell from 41% in 2024 to 23% in 2026. SPF, another email authentication mechanism, was present on 98% of checked domains.

Smaller counties performed worse. Among the third of counties with the fewest residents, 34% of election contact domains lacked DMARC, compared with 12% among the largest counties.

Non-.gov domains also showed weaker protection: 32% lacked DMARC, compared with 16% of .gov domains. These findings indicate an association, not proof that adopting .gov automatically improves email security.

DMARC enforcement can reduce certain forms of domain spoofing, but it cannot prevent every impersonation attempt, lookalike domain or attack involving compromised accounts.

The researchers found 28 websites with consistent HTTPS failures among the 2,081 tested. Fifteen lacked a working HTTPS service, seven presented certificates for the wrong domain, and others had expired or untrusted certificates or failed to establish a secure connection.

Another 178 websites would serve election pages over unencrypted HTTP if visitors requested them that way. Only 34% sent an HSTS header, which instructs compatible browsers to insist on encrypted connections. Sixty-three certificates were due to expire within 30 days of Election Day.

A separate test examined third-party connections when election pages loaded in a clean browser, without clicks or scrolling.

Of 1,930 measured pages, 84% contacted at least one company identified as a tracker by Disconnect or DuckDuckGo. The median page contacted six third-party domains. Google Analytics or Tag Manager appeared on 60% of websites, while Meta Pixel appeared on 3%.

Mysterium suggests that some tracking results from default settings in website platforms rather than deliberate decisions by election officials. The presence of third-party code does not, by itself, establish unlawful tracking or prove exactly what information was collected.

Still, counties should review whether these connections are necessary on pages designed to provide basic voting information.

The study examined recognizable election-related domain names across several extensions, including .gov, .com, .org, .net, .us and .vote.

Researchers identified 2,074 matching names that resolved to an address. Of these, 121 were registered outside government control. Thirty-eight hosted unrelated websites, eight were offered for sale, 73 displayed basic server or hosting pages, and two served gambling or spam content.

The researchers also found 73 counties with a working .gov version of the name used by their non-.gov election website, suggesting that some had secured the official address without completing the migration.

A separate test generated 14,456 single-character misspellings of 77 state and large-county election domains. Researchers found 245 registered variants and identified 26 that served parked, placeholder or unrelated pages after excluding potentially coincidental matches.

The study does not establish that these registrations were malicious or identify their owners. However, a voter who mistypes an address or guesses the wrong domain ending could reach a third-party website instead of an official source.

Across the seven states that decided the 2024 presidential election, 43% of identified county election websites were outside .gov, down from 55% in 2024.

In these states, 26% of election contact domains lacked DMARC, compared with 39% two years earlier. However, 55% still lacked an enforced policy.

The nine states whose 2026 Senate races were rated toss-up or lean in mid-October showed similar concerns: 53% of identified county election sites were outside .gov, while 44% of election contact domains lacked enforced DMARC.

These figures measure website and email configurations. They are not evidence that an election has been compromised.

Mysterium recommends that eligible government organizations complete the move to .gov, redirect old addresses, enforce email authentication policies and configure HTTP-to-HTTPS redirects and HSTS.

Counties should inventory legitimate email senders before tightening DMARC policies to avoid disrupting valid communications. They should also review advertising pixels and unnecessary third-party connections, monitor certificate expiration dates and consider registering defensive versions of their domains.

For voters, the report recommends starting with the state election office listed on USA.gov and following its link to the relevant county website. Voters should avoid trusting unsolicited messages or plausible-looking search results without checking the destination.

If an election-office email comes from an unexpected address, voters should verify it using an independently obtained official telephone number. An unusual address is a reason to check, not proof of fraud, since the study found that some legitimate offices still use consumer email services.

The researchers combined Census Bureau county data with official websites recorded in Wikidata and checked them against CISA’s .gov registry. They tested displayed contact addresses, email authentication records, certificates, redirects, tracking requests and lookalike domains.

The study identified 2,081 election pages, compared with 2,913 in the 2024 manual survey. Automated discovery favored larger counties with better-structured websites, leaving smaller counties underrepresented even though some had weaker protections.

The comparisons indicate progress but are not a perfectly matched before-and-after assessment. Different tests also used different sample sizes, and the tracking analysis measured a single page load from one location.

The observations reflect October 17, 2026, rather than continuous monitoring. The findings provide a useful snapshot of public-facing election website security, but individual results should be rechecked before drawing conclusions about a specific county.

item.title: Volt Typhoon Used Silent Train to Hide Zero-Day Attacks
item.description:
Volt Typhoon used disposable relay chains to hide zero-day attacks on critical systems. Lumen linked Silent Train to at least four zero-days.

Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs has spent three years tracking a covert network it calls Silent Train, which it ties to Volt Typhoon, the China-linked APT group. The cybersecurity firm says the network hid exploitation of software flaws the vendors didn’t know about yet. Black Lotus sent hundreds of victim notifications along the way, and the investigations that followed revealed the exploitation of at least four confirmed zero-days and one likely.

“Volt Typhoon’s Silent Train is a covert network designed to gain and maintain access to the technologies businesses rely on to manage devices, networks and critical operations.” reads the report published by Lumen. “Black Lotus Labs® tracked how the group used rapidly changing chains of compromised infrastructure to conceal its activity while exploiting previously unknown vulnerabilities in centralized management platforms.”

Silent Train first showed up in November 2023, shortly before the first takedown of the KV-botnet, Volt Typhoon’s earlier network of hijacked routers. Activity rose after the second disruption. The group dropped persistent infrastructure and moved to disposable chains of compromised devices that it could rebuild whenever it wanted.

Each session began on a rented server outside the United States. It then passed through another server and compromised small-office routers, home devices and IoT equipment in other countries. Finally, the traffic passed through a compromised device in the U.S., close to the target. This helped the attackers make their activity look like normal local traffic and bypass location-based blocks and IP reputation filters. On average, the chains passed through about four devices before reaching a U.S. IP address. Some used as many as six.

Lumen identified more than 27 types of devices used in the network, including TP-Link routers and Fortinet appliances. Some of these devices had no known vulnerabilities, suggesting that Volt Typhoon may have used previously unknown exploits to compromise them and create relay points.

“We observed more than 27 device classes exploited and used in Silent Train operations, ranging from SOHO and IoT devices like TP-Link routers and Netgear Orbi devices to enterprise platforms like Fortinet appliances and CyberPanel servers.” the report continues. “Some relay device types lack known vulnerabilities, suggesting Volt Typhoon leveraged undisclosed zero-day exploits to set up a single relay in a four-to-six hop chain and indicating a willingness to commit significant resources to protecting future access capabilities.”

The attackers exploited exposed web interfaces and installed only the tools needed to connect the devices through SSH. These included temporary SSH services, keys, configuration files and tools already available on the systems. At the end of each session, they removed all traces of their activity and dismantled the relay chain. Sessions lasted about four hours on average, although some lasted only minutes. The attackers could also build a new chain in less than two minutes, suggesting that they had partly automated the process.

The group worked with strict discipline. New device types arrived about one per quarter, and about one per month during the 2023 and 2024 build-out, always tested outside the U.S. first. Roles never changed: Intelbras modems served only as overseas relays, Netgear Orbi devices only as the U.S. hops facing victims, and the server providers stayed separated by layer too.

By early 2025, enterprise platforms like Fortinet, Cisco, PRTG, Mirth Connect and CyberPanel joined as final hops. They stayed up one to three months and supported several intrusions. The group also added reverse tunnels using the open-source proxies Chisel and FRP, and the old and new methods ran in parallel.

Volt Typhoon used Silent Train only during key stages of its attacks, including exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials and data, and maintaining access to compromised systems. Each session targeted between one and five victims, often just one organization. The activity was carried out by human operators, mainly from Monday to Friday, between 9 a.m. and 10 p.m. China Standard Time. The group also paused operations for several weeks around Chinese New Year.

The group targeted tools used to manage endpoints and networks, as well as SD-WAN systems and other control platforms. These systems can manage hundreds or thousands of devices, allowing attackers to reach many systems without moving through the network in the usual way. This approach also helped them leave fewer traces. After the attacks, investigators found webshells running in memory, stolen credentials, misuse of built-in features such as remote file transfers, and deleted logs.

The four confirmed zero-day campaigns hit Versa Director in 2024, N-able N-central through CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN through CVE-2026-20127, and VeloCloud Orchestrator through CVE-2026-16812. The Cisco bug is a CVSS 10.0 flaw, and the group kept exploiting it well after Cisco disclosed it in February 2026. In the Versa case, the group used an in-memory JAR webshell to limit forensic evidence and reach downstream customers.

The likely fifth is Quest KACE. The campaign hit more than 30 victims and faded after Quest’s October 2025 security updates.

“The campaign affected more than 30 victims, followed vendor remediation timelines and declined after Quest’s October 2025 security updates.” the report states. “Despite limited forensic evidence, the available data supports a moderate-confidence assessment that Volt Typhoon exploited a zero-day vulnerability.”

The actor stayed on the KACE server and used its admin features to take credentials.

Victims include telecoms, government agencies, defense contractors, satellite and emergency communications, universities with ROTC programs, managed service and IT firms, and critical infrastructure such as water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail and aviation. What they share is access to bigger networks or customers. Hawaii, California and Texas were the top locations for several years. Lumen can’t say why, but the pattern fits pre-positioning for a crisis in the Indo-Pacific.

“For enterprise leaders, the lesson is clear: systems with broad administrative reach can become high-value gateways to the entire organization and its customers. Reducing internet exposure, accelerating patching, strengthening access controls and preserving security telemetry are essential to detecting threats earlier and limiting their impact.” Lumen concludes.

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, China)
